utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have the witness, please? [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, did you have a good rest yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will not take a long time for the proceedings this afternoon. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, you may continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you testified that after your resignation, you were put on the waiting list. That means that you were unemployed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But is it also correct that at some point you joined the civilian police at this moment, after the resignation, I mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, to that question, I can give the following answer. There was an attempt, there was a failed attempt, to get me to work for the civilian police in Jablanica. However, as that job was not suited to me, in view of the level of my education, and my qualifications, but even more importantly, the necessary procedure could not be performed to conclude a work contract, because under the then police organisation system, all the policemen regardless of the municipality, that is their work papers, whatever you have to hand over, your work booklet, your education certificates and so on and so forth, all that had to be sent to Sarajevo. As Sarajevo was cut off, I could not get all these papers and they could not be sent through, so after a few days, I realised that nothing would come out of that job.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Who was the person who invited you to work with the civilian police in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could all this -- could we go into private session? I think all such things should be -- should be -- all these questions should not be in a private session because the identity of the witness might be revealed so can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you claimed that it was MOS that started armed conflict in April, 1993, in Jablanica municipality, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And you showed us one document, Exhibit D1/336. And now I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 296.1. There is an error in the transcript, just page 15, line 23, it is written studied. It must be "started," the conflict started. I will direct your attention especially to paragraph 1 and 2. Witness, have you read the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: As you see, it makes reference to the document that was read out yesterday in the courtroom, exhibit that I just named, 336. Is it correct, Witness, to say that it is not -- it was not MOS military actions, it was the attempt of HVO to implement Vance-Owen agreement by force that was the cause of this military conflict? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I have understood the question completely. Especially its first part. I believe that you have asked me several things. Can you please break the whole thing down into several questions? Because I have a feeling that you are leading me into giving you a wrong answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I will make things easier. From this order, from this minutes, I, for example, make a conclusion that it was -- it were attempts of the HVO to implement by force the Vance-Owen agreement that caused the military conflict in the Jablanica area in April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is not correct. This is not correct. I have other information about these facts and my information is confirmed by the text in -- under item 1 of this document, if you will allow me, I know from a conversation with Mr. Matan Zaric and we are talking about 15 April, 1993, when I was informed that the units of the BH Army launched attacks in the region of Doljani, attacks on the HVO units, and that the Muslim civilians were leaving Doljani and starting to go towards Jablanica, which I witnessed myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Now I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 299.1 -- sorry, it's not -- sorry, not that. Exhibit 301.1. This is an order issued on the 16th of April, 1993, by Colonel Zeljko Siljeg. Witness, I would like you to read paragraph 7, 8 twice.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, seven and?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Five. 5, 7, 8. Do you see that on the 16th of April, the date of the operation in Sovici and Slatina was specified by the HVO? On the eve of the operation. Do you agree with me that it was HVO that started the military operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot agree with the statement that the HVO started the military operation, because I already said I have other information. However, I doubt the authenticity of this document. It does not contain the important characteristics of authenticity, and the events on the ground, and my information about those, differ completely from the way you put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, do you see a stamp at the bottom of the page, the stamp confirming the reception of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, so far as I understand, this document has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So there is no need to debate on the authenticity of this document at all with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, you were not present in Sovici on the 17th of April, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was not in Sovici on that day, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How do you know what happened in Sovici on the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to complete my sentence. Yesterday, and today, on several occasions, I've already said and repeated that I was not a soldier, I did not belong to any army, to the HVO or any other army. You are addressing too many questions of the military nature to me. You are insisting on me saying something that only a soldier could know. So how come I know what happened in Sovici? If I need to answer, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How do you know? It's a simple question. You were not present there. How do you know what happened there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very simple question, a very simple answer. When the BH Army, in its terrorist sabotage attack on the 27 July, 1993, attacked Doljani village, and killed nearly 40 civilian Croats, and detained --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the answer, just a moment, this is the answer. You will get it in my next sentence. And they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... speeches and you're not answering the question. The question which we all want to know is how do you know that Doljani was attacked before Sovici on April of 1993? April, 1993. Yesterday, you told us that your brother was in the army or in the HVO and that Doljani was attacked on the 15th of April. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already answered that. I will repeat it. I know that from a conversation with Mr. Matan Zaric and my brother on the 15th of April was no longer a commander of -- because a month before that, he left that duty for health reasons, and I know about the 15th of April from Mr. Matan Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And also on the -- July -- sorry, April in Sovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: 17th April, and the events that happened on that day, I know about them from the detained prisoners, from Doljani, on the 28th of July I spent several months with them in the camp, so we had enough time to go into details.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Who was in command of the operation in Sovici from the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yesterday, you stated that the civilian population was evacuated to Jablanica, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: From Sovici and partly from Doljani.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evacuation of the civilian population from Sovici, I already explained yesterday, and I confirm that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, however, I've already answered that. I answered that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, Witness NE, I have a note of what you said yesterday, and of course my note is subject to what appears on the transcript. But I have a note with a red mark beside it saying that you said that your brother was the commander of the HVO battalion in Doljani. You also gave information about the Muslim forces there, and that you said that you personally saw people leaving the area of Doljani. So now today you are saying that your brother was not in the HVO because he was sick. You don't know who was the commander at Doljani, and further that your information is not from personal observation but following a conversation with -- I have a note, with Mr. Matan Zaric. No, let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry, Your Honour, if the transcript says what I have just heard from Judge Clark. This is not what I said. This is how things were. My brother was the commander of a battalion throughout 1992 and maybe for a month of 1993. So he was certainly not the commander in April, and on the 15th of April, he could not have been in Doljani because he was with me in Jablanica because he was taken prisoner at the same time as me and taken to the camp, and so I didn't say that, or if I was either misunderstood or misinterpreted, this is an opportunity to correct that. On the 15th of April, my brother was not in Doljani but he was the commander of a battalion in 1992 and for a month in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: What is the connection between your brother and Doljani, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The connection between my brother, as the commander of an HVO battalion from Doljani, lies in the fact that the members of the HVO, throughout the entire 1992, the entire 1991, mostly were deployed in Doljani and they would, during 1992, they would be sent to Konjic municipality to man the positions facing the Serbian forces. So this is the connection between my brother and Doljani throughout 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And my final question is: Do you know Mladen Naletilic or did you know him ever before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say I'm very disciplined. That's why I complete my cross-examination at the appointed time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, you should have finished your cross-examination earlier. Anyway, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Shall we make the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It depends, how long are you going to take, if just a few minutes we will continue to sit for a while. But if for a long one, we will have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to -- it's not going to be a few minutes. I would like to clarify, because Judge Clark did not allow me the intervention previously. This is exactly how the witness testified yesterday and I would like to clarify a few things. It's not going to be a few minutes but maybe ten, 15 minutes, so longer than a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. In this case, let's have a break. We'll resume at 4.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I merely wish to say we checked the transcript, on pages 11780, and 11781, the witness said the same thing as today as he said yesterday. Perhaps it was a misinterpretation or -- 11780.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let us try and clear up certain matters. My first question, please be so kind. You said that you learned from Matan Zaric about the attack on 15th of April, how, when, what happened and everything else. Will you please explain to the Honourable Court all these details to the end, because I believe this has not been fully clarified and the Prosecutor asked you about that and also the Judges asked but that. So will you please tell them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That 15th of April, 1993, Mr. Matan Zaric was turned back from the checkpoint at Bokulja, which is at the entrance into Jablanica from the direction of Doljani. He was turned back without an explanation. After that he returned to Doljani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Just a moment, witness, because we need clarification on this, you have to be very careful. Did you see Mr. Matan Zaric being turned back or did he tell you this story?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After he was turned back, he called from Doljani by radio, and explained that he had been turned back. So I heard it from him. He explained that he had been turned back and asked me to check why had that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you please explain it better, what checkpoint, what was he in Jablanica, where did he live? Where was he going? Will you explain it to the court? Because the Honourable Judges do not know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bokulja checkpoint was controlled by the ABiH members and it is between Jablanica and Doljani, at the exit from Jablanica towards Doljani. Mr. Matan Zaric who was a representative of the HVO and was resident of Doljani, he needed to come to Jablanica every day. So that day, the 15th of April, around 10.00, he was turned back from that checkpoint without any reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean he was not allowed to enter Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Members of the ABiH would not let him enter Jablanica. He went back to Doljani, and then by radio, he established contact with me and said to me, [redacted], I have made a mistake."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry could we go to private session and could this be redacted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now I have a couple of questions in relation to the growing tensions in your home town. As I understand it, you described to us how relations between the ethnic communities were good prior to the balance being affected by the influx of refugees. Now, the question I want to ask you is: Were the refugees uniquely Muslim refugees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you know why that was? After all, we know that people of Croatian origin were victims of the aggression in 1992 as well as Muslims. Why were only Muslims coming to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I can't really give you any specific answer. I've explained one of -- possible reasons because in 1992, there were no combat operations of the Serb forces, that is in 1992, there was peace in Jablanica in contrast with Konjic, Mostar and other places, so that was the reason why they lingered on in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that they weren't refugees at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were refugees. I've said that. They were expelled from East Bosnia and let me not repeat it because I've already said that and some places in East Herzegovina so they were refugees. I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The question I asked you is why do you think that there were only Muslim refugees? Why were there no Croat refugees, seeing that both groups suffered equally at the hands of the Serbs in Eastern Bosnia and Eastern Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think -- I mean I know that in East Bosnia, Rudo, Gorazde, Foca, Rogatica, I don't think there are as many as 0.00 Croats. Those places are inhabited by Serbs and Muslims. I don't think there are any Croats at all. So when refugees came from those places, one could not expect to see any Croats among them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. Because I didn't know that. In relation to the tensions which were rising between the two communities, do you see any connection at all between the use of the prefix Croatian in front of many institutions following the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? Do you think that played any role in the increasing tensions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want it to be known that those unfortunate people, the refugees, the Muslims from East Bosnia, could not be irritated by any Croatian prefixes because in Jablanica, these prefixes did not exist anywhere in any walk of life. So I do not think that could vex them, that that could bother them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The other question I wanted to ask you relates to Doljani and Sovici. Did you actually go to Doljani or Sovici at any stage from mid-April to the end of April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can you tell me the last time that you have been in Sovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to Sovici only as late as 1994, after I came out of the camp and went to Mostar, so that was the first of March, 1994, and a few days later, I went up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did you see the condition of the village of Sovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't. I took the road, the road that one usually takes. I wasn't really interested to find out the state of the whole village because the village is rather dispersed, the houses are scattered, they are not grouped in one place. And in that area, through which the road goes, I saw what I could see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd share that information with the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what I'm expected to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Would you mind describing to me what you saw? You said that you saw what you could see. What could you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw -- I saw there next to the road, which I took, that there were houses burned down. It was March, 1994. So it was winter time. So well, one couldn't see anything particular. I mean, it wasn't the agricultural season. It was the time of the year when people would be working tilling the land, you couldn't see at that time of the year people in the fields.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Is it your evidence, Witness NE, that Doljani was attacked by the ABiH on the 15th and your information is because your friend couldn't get into Jablanica? What is the source of your information that Sovici was attacked on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the break, I tried to explain but I was interrupted. The information that Sovici was attacked on the 17th of April, 1993, I received from the detained Croats who were taken prisoners on 27 July in the ABiH Army operation. Besides some civilians, there were also ten or 12 members of the HVO who were together with me in the camp, in the museum camp. We were there for four months. And I had the opportunity to learn that from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So this is the first time that you had heard that Sovici was attacked was at the end of July when you were in a camp. Can I take it from that, Witness NE that during the period from the 17th of April until July, Sovici's attack was a complete surprise to you? You were utterly unaware of any activity between any parties in Sovici on the 17th of April until you heard it on the 27th of July and thereafter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must say that I heard even before that, but these -- this was controversial information. I heard some information on the -- from the press service of the 44th Brigade of the 8th Army of BH, which took over the local civilian television under their wing, and I also heard some other information, which spoke contrary to the fact things actually were, so I did not really believe what I heard. So this is the information that I received from the press service of the 44th Brigade via the local cable TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I take it that that information indicated there had been an attack on Sovici on the 17th of April, and for the days thereafter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You were describing to us, Witness NE, that before the 27th of July, 1993, you had heard something about events in Sovici but because you heard it from the information service of the 44th Brdska Brigada, via local cable TV, that you didn't believe it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not believe this information, as I already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. What I wanted to know is what was the information which you rejected because of its source?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, on the same television, from the same television, while I was still not in the camp but there were other Croats who were detained, I heard that there was no camp whatsoever, that nobody was detained, and I knew that there were people detained because some of my friends were there, and on the television, I heard that there were no camps. That's why I did not trust that television source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I got that point. You didn't believe the information because of the source, and you're giving me another example for the validity of the rejection of the information. But what I'm asking you is what did this source actually say about the events on the days following the 17th of April? Now, I accept that you didn't believe it, but can you recall how the events were described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were described in the following way. It was said that the majority of the Muslim population had been killed, that many were massacred, that unprecedented evil was done, that almost nobody remained alive in Sovici. This is the information that I heard on that television. And I couldn't believe that, especially I couldn't believe it because at the beginning of June, 1993, I personally saw Muslim refugees who were bussed and arrived in front of the SDK building in Jablanica. Since I knew some people, I could tell that not everybody had been killed. And I was then glad that the information was not correct. It was not correct that everybody had been killed, as they said on TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did the television say who in fact had attacked Sovici, who was responsible for these, as you describe, exaggerated events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On TV, it was said that Sovici was attacked by the HVO and that over 90 per cent of the Muslims in Sovici were killed, and that they -- that the major brunt was taken by the civilians. I didn't believe it. I couldn't believe it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me now what your colleagues and inmates, co-detainees told you about the events? Who did they say attacked Sovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleagues, inmates, from Doljani, who were brought over on the 27th of July, told me that since the positions before the conflict, the HVO positions were at lower points, and the Army of BH were at higher points, because of the way the forces were deployed, and because of the number of troops of the respective two armies, they told me that on that particular day, the BH Army had attacked the HVO, which had been surrounded, but that after a certain time, they -- the reinforcement arrived to the HVO forces and the attack was then repelled. It was neutralised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I take it, then, that what you're saying is that there was a skirmish between the two armies and that as a result of the skirmish, the HVO attacked Sovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no skirmish, there was no conflict. The HB army intended, pursuant to the document that I showed you, to eliminate the HVO physically from this area, and this had already started. The checkpoints had been taken over. And then they proceeded towards the north west, in order to expel, to eliminate the HVO from the area of Jablanica municipality, because it had already been done in the municipality of Konjic, which is somewhat further up to the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm having difficulty understanding your evidence but can I put the question a little more simply? Is it your evidence that Sovici was not attacked by the HVO or anybody with similar interests as the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am saying that Sovici was not attacked by the HVO. The situation was absolutely different. All the HVO forces, both in Sovici and in the entire municipality of Jablanica, in the entire municipality of Konjic, were attacked by the BH Army in order to implement the plan of the Operation Neretva 1993, in order to occupy Stolac, Mostar, and further down to the sea. This was done gradually, first in Konjic, then in Jablanica, then further down southwards, but fortunately enough they didn't get all the way to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness NE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There are no questions out of Judges' questions? Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question relative to the question of Judge Clark, why did refugees come to Jablanica, what was the situation in Jablanica. My question is was Jablanica ever shelled? When, if it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Anybody.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Jablanica was shelled in the summer, in July, 1992, by the air force of the former JNA, on several occasions. Luckily enough there were no casualties, there was no major material damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What about artillery attacks in 1993? That's what I meant when I asked you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It was never shelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was still there, when I was still free, before I was detained, I don't know, later on, objectively I could not -- I couldn't know because I left Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When did you leave Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On 8 September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So until 8 September, 1993, no single shell fell on Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. And thank you for coming here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much, Witness, for coming here to give your evidence. We appreciate that very much. When the usher pulls the blinds down, he will show you out of the courtroom. We all wish you a pleasant trip back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and thank you very much for allowing me to say the truth before this Tribunal, because I hope that this will contribute to establishing the whole truth and passing a just and fair judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as for the documents, I hope both parties could file us in three days a list for the documents you are going to tender. At the same time, in another three days, you could file the response to the documents offered by the other party concerning the tendering of those documents. In the meantime, this Trial Chamber would like to invite both parties to submit your views concerning the interpretation of the BiH government. I understand during the proceedings, there is some disputes concerning this terminology. We would like to hear fully the views from the both parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for wise and just decision regarding the position and the difference in interpretation. What I would like to say now is that today this is the 12th or the 13th witness, but the Prosecution is doing the same thing all over again, the same practice. I don't know whether this is actually the practice in Anglo-Saxon system that documents are delivered to the Trial Chamber which are then not used in cross-examination. So the way I interpret this, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. because in my system, and in the system that the President of this Trial Chamber belongs to, I have -- my feeling is that the documents are given to you to read and that it is not important to follow these documents in the cross-examination. About 60 per cent of these documents, which are tendered for the cross-examination, are not actually used in cross-examination. This has been the practice with all the 13 witnesses. I have checked it. And again with this witness, the situation has been the same. Over 60 per cent of these documents have never been presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think we made a decision in admitting the documents. There is a paragraph which clearly stated the position of this Trial Chamber that in principle only those documents introduced or used through a witness could be admitted into the evidence. Otherwise, the parties have to find another way to have those documents admitted. For instance, 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There has been a misunderstandings, I'm afraid. Your Honours, I apologise, I believe that there has been a misunderstanding. I asked for your instruction. I don't know what the practice of this Tribunal is. I don't know what the practice of the Anglo-Saxon system is. Why does the Prosecution give you this binder with, I don't know, 20 documents, gives it to you, and then you take it away to read, and then, in the cross-examination, they will only use two documents and the remainder of the documents stays with you? That was the case today, in the cross-examination the Prosecutor used not more than 35 per cent of the documents. What is the purpose of all the other documents? Why do they put together a binder? Why do they give all the documents to you to read? I'm not talking about the admission of documents, but why the documents are being given to you in the first place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think this question should be answered by the Prosecution. In my view, in my understanding, that it is very difficult to prejudge what kind of documents that will be used during the cross-examination, because it's all depends on the direct examination and what kind of questions or issues may come up during the cross-examination. So in this way, the Prosecution furnished us with a bundle of documents, and frankly speaking, we don't have time at this moment to go through all those documents at all. If you request, and if the other two Judges agreed, we could turn back those documents which were not used to the possession of the Prosecution. There is no problem from this Trial Chamber. Yes, Mr. Krsnik, are we going to have the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What kind of protective measures do you ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Distortion of the witness's face and the pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have the next witness? Your request is granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, Mr. Seric, I understand the point you're making about the bundles of documents and you've probably noticed that I take them out with me, and I do read them. They don't always mean a great deal in the absence of explanation but I think, to put your mind at rest for the future, I won't read any documents unless they are actually introduced, because I myself have wondered why we received so many documents and so few are referred to, although I recognise that it is impossible to predict what a witness is going to say. So to put your mind at rest, I won't read them any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While the witness is being brought into the room, while I was judge, I used to read many more documents than I actually used while I was passing my decisions. To my mind, the situation is absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, since everyone in the courtroom now has addressed this matter except the Prosecution, I think we should have a chance to respond. Your Honour, it is never been my practice in terms of answering Mr. Krsnik's question in terms of the Anglo-Saxon practice and I won't be so bold as to talk about Anglo-Saxon practice, I will talk about American practice, and that is I have never been required to give a bundling of exhibits at the beginning of cross-examination. I've never been that. We've tendered one exhibit at a time as the questions are asked and as the documents are used. It is the practice, and it was at the request of this Chamber that bundles of documents were prepared ahead of time, on best guesses as to what we might be able to use. Now, we don't know how long the witnesses will be. We don't know how responsive they will be. Some day, some day, we may have a witness who gives short answers and responsive answers and we may get through all the documents but many times, as the Chamber has observed itself, the witnesses take a long time to answer the simplest questions and we are simply not able to get through all the exhibits that we prepare. That's the simple answer. It's no more complicated than that. But if the Chamber directs us to continue to submit bundles, we will. I am very happy and we would be only too pleased to go back to a system where we will tender each exhibit one at a time as we go. If the Chamber tells me that, we will change our practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will take note of what you said. Yes. We will have the next witness now. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you can relax. I know that this is your first time ever in a situation like this. I would just like to give you some instructions. The usher is going to show you a piece of paper, and if your name is on that piece of paper, just say, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The next thing I would like to tell you, in front of you is a screen. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you see the cursor that is moving? I'm kindly asking you for the purpose of cooperation, as -- and as efficient examination as possible, since we both speak the same language, please wait until the cursor stops. We have interpretation into English and French. It is very important that we get the best possible interpretation on the screen. Can we please go to the private session? It is very important for the Trial Chamber to receive the information about this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we are not interested in the structure of that house, because that may not be the subject of the issue which is in dispute. All we want to know from this witness is who built that villa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour. That is why I brought this witness, this fact witness, but you know, this is a witness from Siroki Brijeg, so perhaps I thought I might make you more familiar with the atmosphere in Siroki Brijeg, just a little bit. I didn't mean to insist on that too much. And of course my questions will be who built it, and of course my chief question will be the Defence asked to see what the witness knows about it. That's the only reason why I called this witness, because this is one of the counts in the indictment, isn't it? But I believe we have only one more background witness, as far as I know, and all the other witnesses will be short and testifying to specific facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, we broke at a point when you told us that the work began. So will you please tell us when was that and then I will move on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Quite right. I cannot give you the exacts date because I do not really remember it but we started work in November 1992. However, I'd like to seize this opportunity to apologise from the bottom of my heart to the Honourable Court and everybody else here because this is really my first and I hope the last time that I'm in a courtroom. I really do not know how I am supposed to behave so I hope you won't hold it against me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, we appreciate that you're coming to The Hague to give your testimony. Actually, all your doing is to help us, the Judges. So please speak slowly so that whatever you say will be translated into the other two languages. And try to give very short and concise answers to the questions put to you by Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry, I understood what the witness wanted to say. I wanted to apologise to the Chamber that he did not stand up in time and bow to the Honourable Court before the break, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So let's move on. Will you please be so kind as to tell us who did the work, who built the house? Who did the earth works and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: The house was built by companies that we subcontracted, because we had -- we concluded the contract under a turn-key principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you please explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: It means that the investor is interested only in the finished house, the quality of work, and he undertakes to pay for all the work that had been contracted. The majority of works -- work was performed by a local company called MVT Garant owned by Mr. Ivo Vrljic called "Grga" and that company came from Polog. It is from the locality of Polog and all the workers come from Polog. It is about halfway between Siroki Brijeg and Mostar. So we contracted those companies, and we paid them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did the contract include only the house or something else? Will you slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: It also involved the landscaping around the house itself. That is all the earth works, the support walls, and now it occurred to me, when we did these -- the landscaping projects, I suggested, simply because we had to bring earth to that slope because of the natural conditions, and to build a swimming pool. That is only to perform the concrete -- the concrete walls of that -- of that swimming pool, and the investor agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I will now show you an Exhibit, which is 25.6 so show us where was this slope? Where did you have to fill it? And will you tell us if this swimming pool was ever used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: As far as I know, that swimming pool was never put to use because I never received any information as to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you please use the pointer? Now, will you please take the pointer and show what is it that you have to fill and why then the swimming pool and why did you suggest it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Very well. Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, you have to point here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: You can see here the support wall, and you can see the difference. So we had to build this support wall, which is made of natural stone, and then we had to fill it in, in order to obtain flat plateau. So since there was this large cavity, I suggested that we perform basic works, that is to cast the concrete work for the swimming pool, and you see this tree, this is the fig tree which Mr. Naletilic wanted to keep at all cost. And there is also a bolder. So that we adjusted the shape of the pool so as to preserve that tree. And a man who has a company specializing in swimming pools, owned by Mr. Vrljic, helped me with all this so that we cast the concrete shell so that the swimming pool could eventually be put to use, built by building in filters and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, sir, and if this swimming pool was to be filled, with what would it be filled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Look, I have to tell you that in this situation, there was nothing to fill it with because here, above the house, we -- I don't know if you can see it on this photograph --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'll give you another exhibit, which is 25.4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Above the house, about 50 metres away, we used the difference in altitude and we built here a water reservoir, the water had to be brought by water tankers. And in this locality, around, nobody has any water, and we have very many water tankers in Siroki Brijeg because and they are kept very busy, especially in summertime. So the only way was to use this individual water reservoir to tank it, to tank water there, and then, owing to the natural slope, it could then supply the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are there any water pipelines there now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: No, there aren't. To build the water pipelines, to any point here, would cost a great deal of money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We heard that a canal, that is the canal for the water pipes was built only for Tuta's house. It is to the left of the swimming pool. You see along this rim here, that special water pipelines were being -- that is canals were being dug for Tuta's house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: No, that is pure fabrication, nobody could do that. That is all I have to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes. Finish your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: It is impossible to do because if you look at this first photograph, this first photograph here, I'd like to see a civil engineer who can tell us how can one supply water to this house here. That is pure fabrication. I have nothing to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And let us look at the photograph 25.2. It was said, we heard it in the courtroom, that it was -- that the digging was done from the left corner here towards the house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Gentlemen, I was just like to say one thing. This whole hill, Cigansko Brdo, Gypsy Hill and all the surrounding hills are at least 500 metres above the river. Above the sea level? Yes, above the sea level. From day one until the last day I was in this building in the construction site and in full responsibility, I claim that this is a fabrication. There are no water pipes here, nor they can be brought here or done here under these conditions. But anybody can check that on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are there water pipes here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: I already said that there are no water pipes here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Not even the surrounding villages have water supply?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: No, they don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Where is the first village in direction to this house, in respect of this house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: In this direction. I'm going to show you, the first village is Donji Crnac and then Gornji Crnac. I would like to say something else if I may. Not only that the surrounding villages do not have water pipes, water supply, half of the town does not have a water supply. This is the infrastructure that was there during the former Yugoslavia. Nothing has been invested in any other infrastructure, and that can easily be checked. So that in Siroki Brijeg, there are at least 20 water tankers that supply people with water every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The Defence is going to ask for an on site inspection by experts. This has always been the intention of the Defence but I just wanted to hear you because you are also a construction expert who has also built this house. Let's move on to my next question. You may sit down. Tell me, please, who were the workers who worked on the house? Do you know them? Where were they employed? The workers who worked on the house and the environment of the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: I have already mentioned the company MVT Garant who was our subcontractor. So we subcontracted all the works. We gave them the tasks and we made money on our part, and they made money on their part. This company performed 90 per cent of the work on this house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When was everything finished? When was it completed, the month if you can remember the exact and the year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact date but the house was completed in mid-March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: The year was 1993. Don't ask me about any date. The house was completed and moved in immediately upon the completion. Mr. Naletilic and his brother inspected the works. He said he did not have any objections, and they moved into the house immediately there upon. The work in -- on the environment, so the supporting work, and the basic work on the swimming pool, which was my suggestion, went on for another 20 days or a month, but the majority of our works were completed, again I can't give you the exact date but it was mid-April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: After April, did you come to the construction site which was not the construction site but the house? Did you go there in May, June and later on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: After that period, there was some ancillary works, some auxiliary works that had to be done, that is the fencing of the property. Then erecting the gate. You could see that gate easily on the photo. Then the access road built of natural stone. But these works did not require a large workforce, and my involvement, but I can say that from the beginning of May, I came to the house twice or three times a week, and Mr. Miro, Mr. Naletilic's brother, was there every day, together with my foreman. The number of workers was somewhat lower because no large number was no longer required and we didn't want to disturb the people who had already moved into the house. And this lasted, again don't ask me about the specific date, but this lasted for another three or four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, we've heard in this courtroom that, besides the water pipes, the Prosecutor alleged that it was the inmates who built the house and the swimming pool. I apologise if I have interrupted you, I apologise once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that characterisation of the indictment. I can take counsel -- should we wish to visit the issue we can go straight to the indictment and the relevant passages. I don't think it's appropriate to do that it front of the witness but I disagree with the characterisation of the charges in respect of this house as they have just been made by Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may cite that paragraph in the indictment on this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Paragraph 44 of the indictment, Mr. President, which is part of counts 2 through 8. Its works -- it makes reference to the use of Bosnian -- shall I read it, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Makes references to the use of Bosnian Muslim detainees to perform labour in locations other than the front lines, including building, maintenance and reparation works in private properties of the members and commanders of the KB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I didn't want to disturb you earlier and I'm glad that the Prosecution have intervened. I looked at the indictment and my memory of what the witnesses said was that none of the detainees ever set foot on the property. It's that they were outside the property. They were talking about other people's houses and they named names where they carried out building works but I think that as far as Mr. Naletilic's house was concerned, they never got inside the gate. And we established, I think that the swimming pool they were talking about was the municipal swimming pool at Siroki Brijeg and not Mr. Naletilic's private swimming pool. I think I'm right in that. So all we were talking about really were a few people who were helping in very strong sunshine to build canals, drains.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are right, but not fully right. I remember well, and my colleague has reminded me, that the Prosecutor in the examination-in-chief of a witness whose name I'm not going to mention, he led the witness in talking about the works on Tuta's swimming pool, and other witnesses, one of them claimed under the examination of Mr. Scott that from this location, he could see Tuta's house and that this is where he built a water pipe. We can go back to that. I know the exactly the questions and the answers of this witness. Can we give the witness the photo, the Exhibit 25.2? And this witness, this particular witness, said that when he was standing here, he could see Tuta's house and that they were digging water pipes for Tuta's house there and the forced labour was on the swimming pool and the water pipe only and exclusively for Mr. Naletilic's house. That's what the -- that particular witness said in the examination-in-chief conducted by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think it's pointless, Mr. President to argue about what the transcripts say but I disagree with counsel's characterisation on that last point as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, it's not proper, it's not proper to say anything about the testimony by other witnesses in front of this witness. You may ask some questions about that pipeline along this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two things. Firstly, why can't I say with another witness said in this courtroom? Why can't I say that in front of this witness? Why can't I say that Witness A, B, C, said so and so? Second question: If the Prosecutor does not agree with this, then I would like to ask him to withdraw part of his indictment and no longer charge my client with forcing inmates to work on his house and around his house. I hope that we are clear on that, and that the position on that is clear from now on, and I will stop examining my witnesses about that. Let's hear the Prosecution. And if they agree with me that my client, Mr. Naletilic, never forced an inmate to work on his house and around his house, for him, and if he issued a statement to that effect, I will stop questioning, examining my witness. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we don't withdraw the charge or the accusation on that point. I've already read to counsel and to the Trial Chamber precisely what the indictment says in respect of this issue. In our submission, the evidence is -- relevant evidence would go to forced labour, not only in the house, if there were such evidence, but also in the environs of the property in general. So I think that this is a matter for us all to argue about at the end of the case based on the evidence that we have, and I just suggest that we get back to the witness and allow the witness to give his evidence so that we can all argue about what it means and whether the indictment has in fact been proven at the end of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can the Prosecutor at least say that these forced works excluded my client's house and the surroundings of that house? And as for the rest, it may stay. If the Prosecutor insists on that. Let us exclude from that forced labour the house and the surroundings of the house of my client. Let's just deal with that. And then I would be willing to stop my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the Prosecution said, "In our submission, the evidence is relevant evidence that would go to forced labour, not only in the house, if there were such evidence, but also in the environs of the property in general." Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In connection with this problem, let me say -- let me put forth the position of our Defence because Vinko Martinovic is charged with a similar accusation of forced labour. This is a principle question when it comes to the examination of this type of witness. What is it all about? The Prosecutor cannot tell us, "I'm going to read the indictment and please examine the witness within the framework of what I have just read," and in such a way prevents any further examination on the part of the Defence. Why can't the Prosecutor say that? The Prosecutor doesn't want anybody else to interpret my indictment. That's why I'm going to read it. Why can't the Prosecutor say that? Because, for a simple reason. The indictment is not precise. So all the objections of this Defence from day one until today with regard to the indictment are based on the fact that the indictment is not precise. How we are going to argue our case, how can we argue the case where it says in summary, words that this is about something and we don't have any specific, any concrete details? Then the Defence has to be allowed to base its defence on what it heard in the examination-in-chief on the part of the Prosecution, and examine their witnesses on the basis of that. And this is the position of our defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at the very beginning of this afternoon's sitting, I remember that I said we are only interested in one question, that is who built that house. Mr. Krsnik, you may ask these questions -- any questions concerning with this question on that. But you should not mischaracterise the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours. That's why I have brought this witness here, but I get the objections that you immediately accept. Then you warn me. But I am absolutely clear that these objections are aimed at rechannelling the quality of this examination. We have just lost ten minutes. I have brought this witness to tell us who did the works on the house and who did the works around the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. house. That's why this witness is here, and I could have finished with this witness already, and if the Prosecutor were just to say that we would exclude from that the works on the house and the works around the house, and that would be very simple to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, I give you the last chance to express your view on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The Prosecution, Mr. President, did not object to testimony from this witness about whether or not others, prisoners worked in the house. I didn't object to that. And Mr. Krsnik can lead four hours of evidence to show that prisoners, if he can call the evidence, let him bring them all to talk for four hours about whether or not prisoners worked on the house. I never objected. I will not object. I objected to his mischaracterisation of testimony of others that's already been heard in this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think the issue is very clear. You may put your question another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, can we put back the Exhibit 25.2? Your Honour, Judge Diarra, I have to apologise to you, I'm very sorry that I'm not able to say anything to you in French, and whenever I address the Honourable Court, I address the Honourable Judge Clark because I find it for linguistic purposes I find it easier to communicate with her. Don't think that I'm ignoring you. I'm not ignoring you and I apologise for my temperamental gestures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind -- the left corner of this photo, can you show it to me? If the person were standing here, would he see this house from this corner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Gentlemen, you don't have to go there to see that this is impossible. You can tell from this picture that this is impossible. You can see that there is a whole hill standing between these two points. It's impossible. No chance. You can go there and you can see for yourself that it is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, have you personally been here, over the past several years, here between this point and the house, did you walk around here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Yes, I've walked here. A lot of people from Siroki Brijeg go for outings here on weekends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: From this point to the house, is there a canal or a channel either filled in or exposed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: There is no canal or channel. And I would like to say that again. Why don't you go there and see it for yourself? There is simply no canal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: During these months, March, April, May, June, July, did you ever see around the house or at the locality that I'm showing you, did you see an inmate, a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to get up to tell you this because I was -- I took the oath when standing up, and I took my oath really seriously and I would like to say before you that no single inmate ever came even close to this construction site, and I will give my life for that, if need may be. I'm an intellectual, I'm a Catholic, I would not allow that myself. And if somebody were to ask that from me, I wouldn't be here. I know the Naletilic family very well. It's a honourable family, and no single member of that family would allow something like that to happen. I have to add something else. In the transcript, I saw the term Muslims. I think something like that. Bosniak Muslims. In this group that was working on the Mr. Naletilic's house, there were half Muslims and half Croats. This is a company which worked under us before and after. I can give you a list of the buildings that we built, the Zagrebacka Banka building in Mostar. They built for us. Those were people, those were the people who lived together in Polog village. And I can give you their names and if it is in the interests of this Court to check that, you can easily check all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And the final two questions: Were you paid? Unless you have a business secret? And can you give us the value of the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Your Honours, sirs, I can tell you that the project was paid for, first we received an advance payment, and finally, everything was paid and we were all -- we also received all of us received a reward. Me first, and then every single man who participated in the works, and as for the value of the works, you are bringing me into a very embarrassing situation. This is my professional secret. I can't give you the value of the works without the consent of the client who paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Okay. I will not insist on that question. What is the current value of this house, if the owner were to sell it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: You can't sell this house. This -- I can't ascribe any value to it because it was built in such a place that it is just -- it does not a market value. I don't know anybody who would want to buy a house in this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you mean in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: No, I mean on Cigansko Brdo, where there are no other houses, when there is no settlement. This is my profession. I'm a professional, and I wouldn't pay anything for this house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How big is this house, how many square metres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: This house has -- I have to think -- has about 160 square metres. And I can tell you that it has -- if this is important at all -- it has four rooms which are distributed among two brothers and two sisters. It has a living-room, a small kitchen, a dining-room, a bathroom on the ground floor, a bathroom in the attic, and it has a gallery, I apologise, it has a gallery and a room of some 30 square metres which is for joint lunches of the whole family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: With regard to other houses in Siroki Brijeg, is this a small house or a big house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: My house, and I'm not a rich person in Siroki Brijeg, my house is at least 60 per cent bigger than this house, but, sir, and honourable -- Your Honours, this is about the life-style in our houses, are shared by several families. My house is shared by my family, my mother, my father died, and my brother and my brother who lives in Croatia also has a part in this house where he stays when he comes over, over weekends or holidays.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know who the real owner of this house is, then and nowadays, the land and the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: It's the Naletilic family. I was given the project, I was tasked by the Naletilic family, Mr. Naletilic and his brother Miro and their two sisters came and they all chipped in. They all shared ideas. They all gave me minor objections and it was very difficult for me to come up with a final solution because of that. But I would like to add to that the only person who financed the project was Mr. Naletilic because other members of the family are not well off, and I received a personal explanation by Mr. Naletilic that he himself -- he personally would finance the project.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My colleague wanted to ask you the following: These Bosniaks, Muslims, they are your employees -- they are the employees of that company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Yes, they were then and they still are. The salaried employees of that company. They performed at least ten jobs before this project and after this project. I can give you their names, their nicknames, if need may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Naletilic talking to them? How did he act towards the workers who were working around the house? Did you see that personally? Do you see Mr. Naletilic in communication with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Mr. Naletilic came to the construction site very rarely. His brother Miro was there all the time. And Mr. Naletilic told me that he had some things to do in Zagreb, he had a company there and he spent a lot of time there. But whenever he came to the construction site, it was the biggest problem for me, because then the work would come to a halt, then they all started joking, drinking beer, and we -- and we didn't work. And I have to say that. The relationship was more than correct. And I don't have anything else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you give us just one or two names of the workers of Bosniak nationality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And please can this be redacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: If I understand your testimony correctly, the house really isn't worth anything, any money, because it doesn't have some of the basic services, such as water. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Yes. It has no market value except for people who own it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So then, I guess it would have made good sense to try to bring water to this place if it were possible to do so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, yes, but that good sense might cost several million German marks or dollars. That is one can bring water by water tankers for one's whole life and yet find no economic justification to build a water supply system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would the market value of this property increase at all if in fact it did have running water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: I think that the market value of this house would go up if only it were about 200 metres lower, and if it were nearer a road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My question was, sir: If in fact the house had a normal water supply, would it be worth significantly more money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: It would be worth more money but not much more. Yes, it would be more but not much more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you've testified about the company that you formed and that you ran during the war. Were you a civilian throughout the war in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: No. I was not a civilian. I was a civilian from the moment the war between Serbs and Croats stopped, which was sometime June/July, 1992, until June -- end of June, 1993. During that period of time, I was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Then beginning in June of 1993, did you become a soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question? Since when?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Beginning in June of 1993, did you become a soldier? And not a civilian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Yes. Thereabouts, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were you a soldier with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Yes, I was a volunteer in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Which unit did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: My specialty is signals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you have prior experience in signals from the JNA, perhaps your compulsory service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Look, have you finished your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to go to the next question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really do not know where all these questions lead to. This is a classical fishing expedition. Let's go out and see if we can catch something. I do not see what it has to do with the testimony in direct. I never once asked a question about the JNA or anything, nor do I care to know about this. The witness came to testify to some specific facts. My examination took only half an hour. I do not know where this leads to because I see that my learned friend does not know and now he is asking questions to see if he can catch something. I don't see any relevance at all. And what does it have to do with the HVO and if he was in the HVO or wasn't in the HVO, so what? Everybody was in the HVO, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much that you remind me that your direct examination only take about 30 minutes and as we ruled before, we will give equal time to the Prosecution, under cross-examination. As for the questions, Mr. Krsnik, we have come back to this issue once again. I think during the previous witnesses, we, this Trial Chamber, has made a ruling that the cross-examination is not necessarily confined within the questions in the direct examination. The person conducting the cross-examination is entitled to test the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect, and I always hold in high regard your good sense, but I was not allowed to, that I was not allowed to address subjects that were not addressed by the Prosecutor during the direct examination. And I put that to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we will take note of your objections. But we'll stick to the rulings we made before. Mr. Stringer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Despite what counsel said, I actually do think I know where I'm going and I think in about two questions, the Trial Chamber will also know where I'm going.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, I want to get back to this very briefly. The unit that were you a member of, the particular unit within the HVO, do you recall the name of the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Siroki Brijeg Volunteer Home Guard Brigade. It was the first unit that I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The"Dobobrami"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Not"Dobobrami" but Domobrani.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Your duties then as a member of that unit took you away from your work with in your private business that you were trying to run at the same time, I take it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in the beginning, I said that after this unfortunate war broke out, my company worked only now and then, which means that in the company, I had three females, three women, who were under no military duty, and at those times when I wasn't a soldier I worked for the company. But you have to understand another thing. That army is not NATO, it is not an organised army. I repeat that it is the home guard troops, volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I know what the home guard is and I'm not going to ask you about that. My point is this, sir: Beginning in June of 1993, you had duties as a member of this HVO unit, and therefore, you did not spend all of your working hours in your private business, nor did you spend all of your working hours up at the construction site and Mr. Naletilic's house, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. Not all the time. And that is why I pointed out that at that time I'd somehow make it to the building site two or three times a week, but I had my foreman, Mr. Vrljic called "Grga," who managed this with workers, I mean all the auxiliary work because all the -- all the chief building, all the construction, was already done by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, therefore, that during those months, June, July, August, of 1993, if Muslim prisoners were working up there in any of the area of the property, it's possible you would not have known about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Impossible. Sir, I tell you that it is impossible, because my foreman was there and in his -- in his, in that whole team, I mean there were always Muslims and Croats, and they were all duly paid. I would have known it the very moment that anything like that happened. But I put it to you that that very moment, I personally would never do anything at that place, at that site. I said it and I said it standing, because that was the oath that I had given before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No one is accusing you of having done anything wrong, sir, okay? My question is this: You were there only two to three times a week during the summer of 1993. And as a result, you don't know what was going on up there all the time. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Sir, I know exactly what was going on up there. If somebody did something apart from my workers, well, I would have seen it on the spot. I would have seen if somebody had done a job for which I was paid to do. To begin with, I'd see a change, and secondly, I would have been told about that by my foreman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You first met with Mr. Naletilic and his brother in the fall, I believe, of 1992? No, I'm sorry, let me clarify that. You first met Mr. Naletilic in early 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And later, toward autumn of 1992, you had more meetings with him Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. as you began to discuss the construction of his house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Little while ago, I told you we met only a few times, because Mr. Naletilic -- only a couple of times, because Mr. Naletilic, or at least that is what he told me, he very busy he was kept busy by his company in Zagreb and that is why all that had to be done between the investor and the executor all this work, all these affairs were performed by his brother, so it wouldn't be true to say that we met often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mentioned his brother Miro Naletilic. Was Miro Naletilic a military man, a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
