utterances.text: When, sir? I've just explained it, explained it to you. The HVO, since you asked me about the military, there are two periods of time. There is a short period of time during the war against the Serbs, and there was a big void until --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that in my questions to you, sir. Let's confine ourselves to the period of time that you discussed on your direct examination. And let's focus particularly on the autumn of 1992, continuing on through the period of time when the construction was completed, okay? In the autumn of 1992, was Miro Naletilic a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was he a member of the Kaznjenicka Bojna, the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mladen Naletilic, during the same period of time, Mladen Naletilic now, Tuta, he was a military man, wasn't he, in the autumn of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: I never saw Mr. Mladen Naletilic as a military, never, not only then, but generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: He never wore a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: I never saw him in a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: They were based in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Some members of the unit were based at the tobacco station in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Look, in the tobacco station in Siroki Brijeg, there were, or rather in a house, we could call it the small building, was the command of the Domobrani, of the home guards in Siroki Brijeg, and the civil defence, and the medical military service and I know that the Convicts Battalion had their office there. That is all that I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Some of their members were also based it at the Park Hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In most places, the building season is not during the winter months, and yet this house was constructed during the winter months.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Sir, you ought to know that our winters are mild. So there is building going on the year round. In our area, summers are not the best time to build anything because it is very hot. And for your information, we are only about 40 kilometres from the coast as the crow flies. We have the Mediterranean climate there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The terrain on which, in the area of this Gypsy Hill is very rough, rocky terrain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Yes, like the rest of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And looking at this photo, 25.6, I understand that it was in fact necessary to build the house on top of a plateau that was constructed with fill dirt so that the entire plateau had to be raised from the top of the hill in order to build or to have a suitable surface on which to build; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Sir, may I have this photograph once again? And will you then please explain to me precisely what is the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I don't think there is a problem. There is just a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think it's called building a raft.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: In building terms, when you have to build a flat surface, it's called a raft, R-A-F-T, in English any way, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Clark. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Years of litigation in civil engineering cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, during the direct examination you were pointing over to the left-hand side of the photograph, indicating that it was actually necessary to raise the surface in order to create a plateau on which the house was situated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: I see. Now I understand what you mean. Well, I simply have to now deliver you a short lecture on civil engineering, because I can see that you are not particularly familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You don't need to deliver a short lecture. I'm sorry to interrupt but I'm going to be limited to about six more minutes, okay? So we are going to have to take the lecture for another time. The only question is this, sir, the special work that needed to be done to situate the house on this site, I would think, dramatically increased the cost of this building project. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Well, not dramatically. And that is why we, the designers, use brains, you know. If you look at this photograph, the house is built in the front part, away from the supporting wall. A house must have a solid foundations. So one cannot build it on the fill ground. And we did intelligently, when we built the foundations here, we transferred this dirt to this area to level it. And you also have to understand that we have cheap labour. So that the work of this kind does not cost much. I hope I was short and clear, if that is enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, getting back to the terrain itself, this rough, rocky terrain, because of that, is that one of the reasons why it would cost so much money to actually dig a line and to bring water up to the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: I just explained it to you, a little bit earlier, that this whole hill is about 500 metres higher than the place from which one should draw water. I'm telling you that the town, as such, does not have the water supply. I mean water mains are lacking. You know. If we had water mains with some big pumps that could then pump water up there, but for the time being, it is impossible to do it. And we really have good water supply only in the centre of the town. We are talking about central water supply, with all the mains and all that. The problem is not the individual pipe. It all must be part of a system. It must be built into a system. I hope you are following me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The cost of bringing water to that house would have been significantly less if the labour was free. Would you agree with me on that point? If labour was not an item?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Look, it would bring the cost down in any -- yes, of course it would. Because if you don't have to pay for labour, then naturally the cost goes down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, any re-examination? Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, because I am always happy to leave sometime for you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Interpretation] Just two things to clear up which I think are vague. Did you use a system that Judge Clark mentioned or did you use solid foundations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: I said very clearly that the house was built over a solid foundation. That is the only way possible to build it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And is the problem -- when we talk about the water supply system, is labour the only problem? That is, that labour who will dig it manually? Or can one use the machinery to do that? And besides, you're a civil engineer so tell me, to build a water supply system there, if Siroki Brijeg has a water supply system, would that then solve or make easier the problem for the villagers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik I have to explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, please explain it to the Chamber, the water supply?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: The water supply system is a system, and it has its primary installations, that is the mains and secondary wells, or to make it simple, pipes, pipes are large diameter pipes as prescribed and we must have hydraulic pumps and that is the prerequisite for the further development of any water supply system. Now in all this, the share of labour is very small. In the overall effort. What costs are the reservoirs, the pumps that will pump this water to higher elevations, that is -- special lines in our area but in Siroki Brijeg, the problem is that we lack this chief, central reservoir, we do not have the mains which would supply the whole territory of the town. And only one part of the town has running water the year round. All the other parts, and especially in summer months, the largest part of the town does not have any running water, not let alone something that is about 500 metres higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, yes, I think I understand. And I believe that Their Honours understand it too. Thank you very much. I have no further questions, thank you for coming?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Questions from the Judges? Judge Diarra?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Witness, I'd like to know after the building was constructed, did you visit -- you said that during the construction, you visited the site two or three times a week, but after that, did anything -- did you have any reason to go to the building, to see what was going on with regard to the maintenance, that is repair, gardening work, and so on and so forth? That is, was there any means of knowing who were people who were there at the time when members of Mr. Naletilic's family there to perform those jobs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: I'll try to be very brief. Any -- any facility, any building, any project, that we finished, we are also bound by our contract to, with in the warranty period, which is about two years usually, once we finish with the works, there are always some minor fill -- minor breakdowns that we undertake to remove at our cost. And I believe this is a very good question. I remember specifically in the case of this house, for instance, the pipes were clogged and we had the problem that some windows were not watertight and we had some problems on the roof because it was leaking. And we are bound by contract, or rather I am bound, to put all these things right within -- for two years. As for the maintenance which you mentioned, Mr. Naletilic's brother, whom I know very well, he looked after the maintenance but it came down to mowing the grass. The grass, if you saw the photograph, that was about it. But for two years after the completion of the construction, it is our duty to remove all the breakdowns and to put them, to repair it all. So I hear that the bathroom is not working because a water pipe is clogged, so that is my mistake. That is the mistake of people who did that. But ultimately it is my mistake and I'm contract-bound to remove all such breakdowns, not only in the case of that house. We always do rounds of all the buildings because after one completes the building there are always some unforeseeable breakdowns or failures that one can not foresee whilst the construction is going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm ask the interpreters for five more minutes sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I'll try to be very brief. I understood you to say, sir, that your works were completed in accordance with the contract, subject of course to any fault that is were reported by mid-April when the family moved in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: By mid-April, by mid-April, approximately, I can't really say that it was the 15th, for instance, but by mid-April, we've finished the main works, and what else we had to do? We had to build the supporting walls, the auxiliary ones, the gate, the fence around the property. Then if you could see the photograph, the access road, which is -- for which we used flag stone, the stone that we found there, and these were all supplementary works performed by two or three men. And they had nothing to do with the building itself, the building could be used at that time. So this kind of work lasted for another two or three months slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think you've answered my next question. I wanted to know were the works after the house was totally completed and the family had moved in which included the fencing the gates and the access road, was that part and parcel of your building contract?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Of the border area? And then the answer is yes. I was responsible for the whole project. Including that and it was done by my men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: We have to watch the clock. The next question I wanted to ask you is was there a septic tank attached to this house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And how did you pipe the waste from the house to the septic tank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: I can explain that if I'm -- if I can see the photograph again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: What I wanted to know basically was the septic tank on the plateau or was it on a lower level? So was the piping downwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: The septic tank? The septic tank, is if you noticed the woods to the right of the plateau, that is the lowest point, and that is where the septic tank is. And that is where the -- that is the points up to which we built in pipes. I can show it to you on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So I take it the pipes were dropped into channels that had been excavated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Not were, they were dug as the building was constructed, because we have to also build all the pipes into the -- into the building. We cannot build a house first and then break it down to build in pipes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I want to you answer my questions simply because all the interpreters and stenographers are here beyond the normal time. How did you pipe the water from the reservoir that you told us that you constructed and that was filled on a regular basis by water tanks? How did you pipe that water to the house? Did that go through channels?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Through channels, which we had to dig before we built the access road. These pipes go next to the access road, if you remember the photograph, and it is clearly marked, and that is how it has to be done. In case such a pipe burst then we have to know its exact location. So if you want me to give you the technical details about the type of the of pipes then I will be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: When you say that this house does not have a water supply what you meant was that it was not connected to a main water supply, not that it didn't have water on tap and all the luxury that goes with running water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Of course, but I thoughts that was clear. There was no outside water supply from the main system. I explained that the water is tanked into the reservoir and then we used the natural slope to bring it to the house, and I said that there were bathrooms in the house, so it's all clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So this house then I would suggest to you was in no different a situation than 90 per cent of the other houses in the country side around Siroki Brijeg. That one built a stone reservoir or a tank. One had it filled by a tanker and one built channels to sluice the water to inside the house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: I think if you knew what the area looked like, then you would understand what I was trying to say. That house has a narrow, stone-paved access road. Not every car can reach that house, you know. I mean there is no asphalt road leading to that house. And that is the basic thing. Nor will it ever be built.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It's a fairly isolated location, is that you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You've been very helpful, thank you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, excuse me, because of the questions posed by Her Honour, that permits us to say how much the building cost. So perhaps it would be interesting. How much did he pay for that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NF
utterances.text: Well, once again, I can not remember the exact figure, Your Honours. I really do not remember the exact figure but the value of the works was about [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be redacted, please because I've forgotten. It is after all a business matter so can the figures be redacted from the transcript, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I've forgotten. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination on this particular question, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Witness, for coming here to give us your evidence. We all wish you good success in your future. Later on, when the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of the room. We all wish you a good trip back home. We'll resume tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 7.12 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 30th day of May, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
